Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed
issues.explanation: For an 18-year-old whose index trauma is witnessing domestic violence in childhood, this appraisal is hard to reconcile with the likely role in the trauma. A child witness may feel guilty, but 'I should have protected others' implies a level of responsibility and agency that is clinically implausible enough to question for this trauma context. The rest of the profile coheres around fear, helplessness, fragmented sensory memory, and hypervigilant threat monitoring; this single appraisal stands out as inconsistent with the demographics/trauma role.

vignette: Jalen, an eighteen-year-old African-American police officer, first came to the station at the age of fifteen, eager to prove himself and protect the neighborhoods his parents had raised him in. His childhood, however, was punctuated by a single, relentless night of domestic violence that would later become the seed for the spirals that govern his present. In the dim light of his bedroom, he watched a mother and a father-a man whose face was distorted by rage-bargain over money while the mother screamed. The scene, which Jalen recalls as a series of stark, vivid snapshots, was punctuated by the sudden thud of a wooden spoon and the sharp sting of a dropped glass. After the incident, the house felt too quiet, too still, and the air carried a tension he could not name. From that moment, the mere presence of suspiciously quiet crowds, or an unplanned touch from a stranger, would immediately drag him back into those dark, cramped memories. The discomfort he feels when someone looks at him suspiciously or when a casual brush of a shoulder makes his heart race is the trigger that brings his memories to life; it forces the images of that night-snapshot memories of a broken chair, a shattered window-to flood his mind. The bodily reenactment is vivid: his chest tightens, his knees buckle as if he were once again standing in that cramped bedroom, his body moving into the same tense position he had assumed when the glass shattered. The grief that follows the recall is overwhelming; he remembers the loss of safety, the feeling that his own life had been irrevocably altered. The negative appraisals that have grown around this core experience compound the cycle. Jalen has convinced himself that he cannot rely on himself, that his own judgment is unreliable and that the world is constantly threatening. These thoughts heighten the sense of threat even in ordinary settings: he feels the presence of danger whenever there is an unfamiliar place, whenever silence lingers too long, whenever any object might be a weapon. The belief that he is "going crazy" feeds into the very images he seeks to escape. Each time a trigger surfaces-a suspicious glance, an unexpected touch-his negative appraisals flare, making him believe that he must always be on guard. The heightened threat perception in turn triggers memory recall; he suddenly remembers the night's violence, the exact sound of the spoon, the weight of the glass in his hands. Memory then amplifies the negative appraisals, reinforcing the idea that he cannot trust himself. In addition, the memory itself can act as a trigger: the sight of a quiet street at dusk, a lone parking lot, or a close proximity to a stranger's shadow immediately brings those images back, which in turn heighten his sense of danger. Threat also makes him more sensitive to triggers; the moment he senses a potential weapon-a metal pole, a firearm-his mind instantly goes back to that violent scene, and his body automatically prepares for a fight. The loop tightens as threat feeds memory, memory feeds negative appraisals, negative appraisals feed threat, and threat fuels every trigger. At the police academy, Jalen's symptoms manifested most clearly on the job. During traffic stops he avoids any unfamiliar vehicle, pausing so long that officers question his diligence. On patrol, he keeps a safe distance from strangers, his eyes scanning for any suspicious posture or potential weapon. The silence that follows a suspect's hesitant cough makes him jump, and he finds himself repeatedly listening for an unheard alarm in the background. His avoidance behaviors spill over into his personal life: he declined invitations to family gatherings because he could not stand the risk of being touched unexpectedly by a cousin's son, fearing that the casual brush of a shoulder would trigger the same body's tightening as if the spoon had fallen again. In the weeks after the accident, these patterns began to erode his performance. He missed a critical shift because he could not focus on the radio conversation, and his supervisor grew concerned. The workplace consequences became a new source of helplessness, reinforcing his belief that he could not control the outcome of his actions. When Jalen finally scheduled an appointment at the mental health clinic, he was tired of the constant mental cross-fire that left him exhausted and alienated. He wanted to stop the loop that made him feel trapped in his own mind and to regain the sense that he could trust himself. His greatest fear remains the idea that he will "go crazy" if he does not find relief, yet his hope is that he can once again walk down a street without the echo of the night's violence haunting him, that he can serve his community without the weight of a lifetime of false alarms. The present moment marks the beginning of a journey to untangle the knots of memory, threat, triggers, and negative appraisals that have bound him for so long.
